flashcards.q: What is an idempotent operation?
flashcards.a: An operation where doing it once and doing it over and over end in the same result.
flashcards.more: Setting `status = 'paid'` is idempotent: ten times over, the status is the same. `balance = balance - 50` is not, because each run takes off more. Requests arriving twice over a network is normal, so the goal is to make every write idempotent.

flashcards.q: What is an idempotency key, and who makes it?
flashcards.a: A unique identity for one job (usually a UUID). The client makes it and sends it in the `Idempotency-Key` header.
flashcards.more: It works like a check number. The server records the key, and when the same key returns it knows this isn't a new job but another try at the earlier one. The server can't be the one to make the key: if the reply is lost, the client would never learn it.

flashcards.q: What does the server return when a request comes again with the same idempotency key?
flashcards.a: It skips the work and returns the first attempt's stored status code and body exactly.
flashcards.more: This is called response replay. From the client's side it looks as if the request just succeeded, yet the real work happened once on the server. That's why the key row has to store the first reply's status and body.

flashcards.q: Why store a request fingerprint?
flashcards.a: To catch a different request (another amount or recipient) arriving under the same key; it is turned away with 422.
flashcards.more: The fingerprint is a hash of the method, path and body. Without it, a client bug sending a $500 request under the same key would get the old $50 "success" back, and the client would think $500 had gone through.

flashcards.q: When two requests with the same key arrive together, what stops the work from running twice?
flashcards.a: A unique constraint on `(scope, key)`: only one INSERT succeeds, and the other waits and gets the stored reply.
flashcards.more: If you SELECT first and see "no key", then INSERT, both requests can see "no". So you run `INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` straight away: 1 row inserted means you own the job, 0 rows means someone else got there first. More in [[concurrency/atomic-operations/oversold-stock|atomic operations]].

flashcards.q: Why are the key row and the real work kept in the same transaction?
flashcards.a: If the work fails, the key rolls back too, so a retry can try again; if it succeeds, the key and reply persist together.
flashcards.more: If the key were committed first on its own, a failure halfway through the work would leave the key behind with no reply. A retry would see "key exists" although nothing was done, and the transfer would be stuck forever. One transaction never creates that in-between state.

flashcards.q: When should a client make a new idempotency key, and when keep the old one?
flashcards.a: New key for a new job or a changed form. Same key when retrying the same job (timeout, network error, 5xx).
flashcards.more: The key belongs to the user's intention, not to an attempt. The classic mistake is calling `crypto.randomUUID()` inside the `fetch` call itself, so every retry gets a new key and the server's protection is useless.

flashcards.q: How long should idempotency keys be stored?
flashcards.a: At least 24 hours, longer than a client can keep retrying. After that, delete old rows.
flashcards.more: Delete too early and a late retry will be treated as new work. Keep them forever and the table grows for no reason. A regular cleanup job removes old rows using the `created_at` column.

flashcards.q: Which HTTP methods are naturally idempotent, and which needs an idempotency key?
flashcards.a: `GET`, `PUT` and `DELETE` are naturally idempotent. `POST` is not, so `POST` needs the key.
flashcards.more: `PUT` sets the whole value and `DELETE` removes something, so doing either a second time leaves the same state. `POST` creates something new each time. `PATCH` depends on what it does: "set a value" is safe, "increase" is not.

flashcards.q: What is a webhook, and why can't you trust it without verification?
flashcards.a: A POST an outside system sends to your URL when something happens. The URL is open, so anyone can pose as the gateway and send fake news.
flashcards.more: When money arrives, the payment gateway tells your server about it, and that call is the webhook. But the URL is open on the internet, so a body that says "paid" is not necessarily true. You need a signature to prove who sent it.

flashcards.q: How is a webhook verified with an HMAC signature?
flashcards.a: The gateway sends an HMAC of the timestamp and body under a shared secret. The server builds the same hash with its own secret and compares.
flashcards.more: Only the gateway and you hold the secret. So being able to produce the right hash proves you know the secret, and therefore that the sender is genuine. Change one character of the body and the hash changes completely, so tampering in transit is caught too.

flashcards.q: When comparing signatures, why `hash_equals` and not `===`?
flashcards.a: `hash_equals` compares in constant time, so an attacker can't guess the hash character by character by measuring response time (a timing attack).
flashcards.more: A plain `===` stops at the first mismatch. An attacker can measure tiny differences in response time and work out the right signature step by step. `hash_equals` always takes the same time.

flashcards.q: What is a replay attack on a webhook, and how do you stop it?
flashcards.a: Capturing a genuine sealed request and sending it again later. Stop it by putting the timestamp inside the seal and rejecting anything older than five minutes.
flashcards.more: A signature, once made, is genuine, so it still looks valid when sent again later. If the timestamp is also an input to the hash, the attacker can't change it, and the server can check that the request is fresh.

flashcards.q: Why shouldn't a webhook endpoint do slow work (emails, ERP calls)?
flashcards.a: The gateway gives up after a short wait and resends the same event. So only verify and store, return 200, and leave the rest to a queue.
flashcards.more: In the controller, do just this: verify, store the event, dispatch to Messenger, then answer 200. The real work happens in a worker, so a slow job never holds the gateway's connection open, and if it fails the worker handles it with its own retries.

flashcards.q: How does a handler stay safe when the same webhook event arrives twice?
flashcards.a: A unique constraint on event_id plus an UPDATE guarded by `processed_at IS NULL`. If 0 rows change, it was already handled: just return.
flashcards.more: Gateways deliver at least once, so the same event can come more than once and the handler must be idempotent. Insert the event id into the ledger only once and mark it "done" only once; both rest on the database's uniqueness guarantee.

flashcards.q: Webhooks don't always arrive in order. How do you handle that?
flashcards.a: Don't set the status directly; use a state machine where only forward transitions are valid. Drop old news when it arrives.
flashcards.more: If a late `pending` event drags a `succeeded` payment backwards, you have a problem. A list of valid transitions rejects that. If you're really unsure, ask the gateway's API for the payment's actual current state.

flashcards.q: When should a webhook endpoint return 500, and when 200?
flashcards.a: 200 once you have stored the event, even if its type is unknown. 500 if storing fails, so the gateway sends it again.
flashcards.more: 200 means "I have this safely, don't send it again." If you reply 200 to news you couldn't keep, it is lost for good. And for a bad seal, reply 400/401, since a retry from the genuine gateway wouldn't be needed here.

flashcards.q: A webhook event arrives before the payment is ready for it. Why not just drop it?
flashcards.a: The gateway will not send it again. If you drop it and mark it processed, the payment stays stuck. Roll back and retry instead.
flashcards.more: A `succeeded` event can arrive before the reply with the gateway id has been saved, or a `refunded` one before `succeeded` is applied. Compare the payment's state with the event's target: if the payment is behind it (or not found yet), throw so the claim is rolled back and Messenger retries with backoff. If the payment is already at or past the target, the event is old news, so drop it.

flashcards.q: What is the risk if a payment's status is just a string column?
flashcards.a: Anyone can set any status, so succeeded goes back to pending, or a failed payment gets refunded. Nothing stands in the way.
flashcards.more: With `setStatus()` called from ten places in the code, there are ten places to make a mistake. A state machine brings these rules into one place, so a wrong change can't run at all.

flashcards.q: What is a state machine?
flashcards.a: A diagram fixed in advance: which states exist, and which named paths lead from one state to another.
flashcards.more: The thing is in exactly one state at a time. Each path from one state to another has a name (such as `succeed`). A path that isn't in the diagram can't be run.

flashcards.q: What is a terminal state? Give examples from a payment.
flashcards.a: A state with no transitions out of it. For example failed and refunded.
flashcards.more: The benefit of a terminal state: old or late events can't change it. The work is finished, and if anything more needs to change, you create a new record rather than altering the old one.

flashcards.q: Why is there no direct path from `created` to `succeeded` in the payment diagram?
flashcards.a: Because you can't assume the money came without asking the gateway. `pending` sits in between to mean "we don't know".
flashcards.more: Without a pending state, there'd be no way to show "sent, but no answer yet", and after a timeout we would just assume success or failure. That is the biggest mistake with unknown outcomes, covered in [[payments/unknown-outcomes/timeout-not-failure|the next segment]].

flashcards.q: In Symfony Workflow, what is the difference between the `state_machine` and `workflow` types?
flashcards.a: In a `state_machine` the thing is in only one place at a time. The `workflow` type allows it to be in several places at once.
flashcards.more: A payment needs exactly one state, so state_machine. If you have several parallel steps (say "verify photo" and "verify address" running together), you need the workflow type.

flashcards.q: What do `can()` and `apply()` do in Symfony Workflow?
flashcards.a: `can()` tells you whether a transition is legal from the current state. `apply()` changes the status if it is legal, and throws if it isn't.
flashcards.more: apply() changes only the in-memory object; you need a flush to write to the database. So for events from outside, check with can() first. Calling apply() directly on an illegal transition throws a `LogicException`.

flashcards.q: What goes wrong if two workers run transitions on the same payment at once, and how do you fix it?
flashcards.a: Both see pending and think it is legal, so the last writer wins. Fix: bind the read and write together in a transaction with a pessimistic lock or an optimistic version.
flashcards.more: `LockMode::PESSIMISTIC_WRITE` runs SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, so the second worker waits. When it gets its turn it sees the new status, and its can() returns false. The alternative is a `#[ORM\Version]` column: on a conflict the flush throws, and you retry.

flashcards.q: Why must a transition's history (the audit log) be written in the same transaction?
flashcards.a: So you never end up with a status that changed but no log, or a log entry but no status change.
flashcards.more: With money, losing the answer to "who changed this, when and why" makes disputes impossible to settle. If the two are written in separate transactions, a crash in between leaves them out of step. `audit_trail` only writes to the log file; you keep the database history in the same transaction yourself.

flashcards.q: After a timeout, how many outcomes can a payment call have?
flashcards.a: Three: the work succeeded, it failed, or we don't know. A timeout only says that no reply came.
flashcards.more: There are two reasons a reply gets lost: the request never arrived, or it arrived and the work was done but the reply got lost on the way. From outside, the two look identical, so you can't decide anything from a timeout.

flashcards.q: What can happen if you treat a timeout as "failed"?
flashcards.a: The money may have been taken while the app keeps it failed. The customer tries again and is charged twice, or the money is taken with no record.
flashcards.more: There are two kinds of damage: the customer is charged twice, and your books say "failed" while the gateway's say "succeeded". Reconciliation will catch that mismatch later, but by then the complaint has already arrived.

flashcards.q: What can happen if you treat a timeout as "succeeded"?
flashcards.a: The goods or service go out even though the money was never taken, and the business loses.
flashcards.more: If the request never reached the gateway or the card was declined, an app that assumes "success" ships the order anyway. That is the same as giving the goods away free. So you need a definite answer from the gateway before saying success or failure.

flashcards.q: Why does a payment need a `pending` state?
flashcards.a: It is the home for "I don't know". It makes no wrong decision either way, and you can verify later.
flashcards.more: Without pending, you'd have to force an unknown outcome into succeeded or failed. With pending, it simply means "waiting", and you can easily query which payments are waiting to be verified.

flashcards.q: What are the three ways to learn the real result of an unknown payment?
flashcards.a: The gateway's webhook, a status query you make yourself, and a regular reconciliation job. Keep all three.
flashcards.more: A webhook is fast but can be lost. A status query is under your control. Reconciliation or a sweeper catches every remaining gap. With all three in place, no payment stays pending forever.

flashcards.q: What should the idempotency key be when retrying after an unknown outcome?
flashcards.a: The same key as the earlier attempt. A new key is new work to the gateway, so the money could be taken again.
flashcards.more: Make the key once when the payment is created and store it in the database; don't make it at attempt time. With the same key, if the first attempt succeeded the gateway returns the earlier reply, and if it didn't, the work now happens once.

flashcards.q: Why is a payment committed as pending before calling the gateway?
flashcards.a: So that if we crash mid-call, the ledger still shows that a call was in flight, and the payment can be found for verification later.
flashcards.more: If you call first and write afterwards, a crash leaves money taken at the gateway with nothing in our ledger, and nobody can find that payment. Write first, and the sweeper will catch it.

flashcards.q: What do you do when a status query says the gateway doesn't recognize the reference?
flashcards.a: The call never reached the gateway. Sending the charge again with the same idempotency key is safe.
flashcards.more: If the gateway really never got the call, the work will happen for the first time now. If a call turns up late from somewhere else, the same key means the gateway won't do the work a second time. The result is the same either way, so it is safe.
